entry.title: arXiv open questions — 2026-08-20 — 10 papers, 53 questions
entry.content:
arXiv open questions — 2026-08-20

185 new papers, 165 unseen, 45 shortlisted, 10 kept.

Part 1 — open questions (53, 42 approachable)

  1. When autonomous specialists each decide whether to invest in self-assessment before bidding for a task, under what conditions does value-of-information reasoning shift surplus from the mechanism to strategic bidders rather than improving allocative efficiency?
    approachable — Can be studied in a self-written auction simulation with synthetic Gaussian signals
    from Pandora's AI Model Routing Box: Efficient Allocation with Costly Value Estimation
  2. Do decentralized bidding markets with costly self-assessment remain incentive-compatible and stable when many specialists adopt the same value-of-information policy, or does correlated bidding produce herding and price instability?
    approachable — Population-level agent-based simulation of the bidding mechanism is writable in weeks
    from Pandora's AI Model Routing Box: Efficient Allocation with Costly Value Estimation
  3. How do routing policies based on a Gaussian signal model degrade when specialist value distributions are heavy-tailed, correlated across specialists, or nonstationary over time?
    approachable — Requires only simulation plus public multi-LLM benchmark scores
    from Pandora's AI Model Routing Box: Efficient Allocation with Costly Value Estimation
  4. Does repeated routing among a fixed pool of specialists cause monoculture, where a few models capture most queries and the diversity benefit of heterogeneous systems erodes?
    approachable — Measurable in a longitudinal simulation over public benchmark specialists
    from Pandora's AI Model Routing Box: Efficient Allocation with Costly Value Estimation
  5. Can strategic specialists learn to misreport self-assessments over repeated interactions with a router, and what audit or pricing rules detect such misreporting from allocation logs alone?
    approachable — Learning agents against a router can be implemented with open models and small compute
    from Pandora's AI Model Routing Box: Efficient Allocation with Costly Value Estimation
  6. How do these routing and bidding policies perform in a live deployment with real user traffic, latency constraints, and evolving specialist inventories?
    not approachable — Needs production serving infrastructure and proprietary traffic data
    from Pandora's AI Model Routing Box: Efficient Allocation with Costly Value Estimation
  7. Does restricting evidence visibility among communicating LLM modules still favor generalizing, reusable interfaces as the number of agents grows well beyond four cells, and how does the effect scale with society size and relay topology?
    approachable — Small frozen-LM plus LoRA societies can be re-implemented and scaled modestly on public models with modest compute
    from What You Can't See Is What You Learn: Restricted Evidence Visibility Favors Compositional Generalization in Shared-Genome Language-Model Societies
  8. Do the value-indexed, transplantable communication packets that emerge under restricted visibility survive in non-fixed, learned or dynamic communication topologies rather than a fixed relay?
    approachable — Requires only modifying the relay/attention mask in a self-written training setup
    from What You Can't See Is What You Learn: Restricted Evidence Visibility Favors Compositional Generalization in Shared-Genome Language-Model Societies
  9. Why did all trained societies fail ordinary-language preservation, and can training protocols be found that retain general language ability while acquiring a compositional relay interface?
    not approachable — Diagnosing and repairing degradation of general language ability likely needs larger-scale training and evaluation infrastructure
    from What You Can't See Is What You Learn: Restricted Evidence Visibility Favors Compositional Generalization in Shared-Genome Language-Model Societies
  10. Can the intervention battery used here (same-value packet transplants, destructive ablations, counterfactual packets) be developed into a general observability method for auditing whether inter-agent messages in larger multi-agent systems carry reusable, semantically indexed content?
    approachable — Method transfer and evaluation on open multi-agent frameworks needs only public models and simulation code
    from What You Can't See Is What You Learn: Restricted Evidence Visibility Favors Compositional Generalization in Shared-Genome Language-Model Societies
  11. Would the restricted-visibility advantage replicate on tasks other than sealed natural-language function composition, and does it hold above the preregistered accuracy floor with different base models?
    approachable — New task suites and open base models are publicly available; compute needs are small with frozen LM plus adapter
    from What You Can't See Is What You Learn: Restricted Evidence Visibility Favors Compositional Generalization in Shared-Genome Language-Model Societies
  12. How does memory correlation bias scale as the number of agents sharing a memory store grows — does the false-majority effect worsen superlinearly with population size and shared upstream sources?
    approachable — Can be studied with a self-written multi-agent memory simulation over synthetic provenance graphs
    from Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
  13. Can memory correlation bias, and the effective number of independent evidence sources, be measured from interaction/provenance logs alone as a monitoring signal for a deployed multi-agent system?
    approachable — Requires only logs from a locally run agent system plus network/statistical analysis
    from Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
  14. Does correlation-aware arbitration reduce population-level pathologies such as herding, information cascades and belief monoculture, beyond improving per-query benchmark accuracy?
    approachable — Testable in an agent-based simulation with shared memory, no proprietary data needed
    from Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
  15. How robust is provenance-based correlation estimation to adversarial agents that forge or launder provenance metadata to manufacture apparent independence?
    approachable — Adversarial agents can be scripted in a simulated memory-sharing environment
    from Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
  16. What is the retrieval-cost versus arbitration-reliability trade-off of active evidence recovery when applied across thousands of agents and long time horizons?
    not approachable — Long-horizon large-population LLM agent runs need substantial inference compute budget
    from Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
  17. Does distilling aggregate destination composition into an LLM agent policy generalise beyond stadium egress after sporting events, to other event types, cities, or transport modes?
    approachable — public OD/mobility datasets and open LLM fine-tuning at small scale suffice for a replication study
    from Distilling Aggregate Mobility Statistics into a Language Model Policy for Post-Event Crowd Simulation
  18. How much individual-level behavioural realism is recoverable from aggregate counts alone, and what identifiability limits govern which behaviour rules are distinguishable given only zone counts and OD flows?
    approachable — can be studied by generating synthetic ground-truth trajectories in a self-written simulator and testing recovery
    from Distilling Aggregate Mobility Statistics into a Language Model Policy for Post-Event Crowd Simulation
  19. Are there correction schemes better than iterative proportional fitting plus resampled fine-tuning for counteracting the dominant-class inflation introduced by fine-tuning on aggregate targets?
    approachable — small LoRA fine-tuning experiments on open models are within reach of a single researcher
    from Distilling Aggregate Mobility Statistics into a Language Model Policy for Post-Event Crowd Simulation
  20. Does matching aggregate destination shares also improve downstream simulation outcomes such as congestion, crowd density peaks, or evacuation times, rather than only the fitted statistic?
    approachable — requires only a pedestrian simulator the researcher can write and public event data
    from Distilling Aggregate Mobility Statistics into a Language Model Policy for Post-Event Crowd Simulation
  21. How does the calibrated crowd policy behave when many such agents interact and adapt to congestion, i.e. do aggregate-fitted policies remain valid under endogenous crowd feedback?
    approachable — multi-agent simulation loop is implementable locally
    from Distilling Aggregate Mobility Statistics into a Language Model Policy for Post-Event Crowd Simulation
  22. Can the aggregate-to-policy distillation be validated against real individual trajectories to quantify residual error, and what privacy guarantees does the aggregate-only pipeline actually provide?
    not approachable — needs privileged access to individual mobile-network trajectory data
    from Distilling Aggregate Mobility Statistics into a Language Model Policy for Post-Event Crowd Simulation
  23. Do step-level credit signals (LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, policy confidence) fail to track causal contribution in multi-agent or multi-turn interactive environments as they do in a single-agent tool environment?
    approachable — Can be run with open-weight agents in a public multi-agent simulation the researcher writes
    from Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
  24. Can a credit-assignment signal be constructed that beats chance at identifying causally pivotal decision points, e.g. by using cheap partial replay rather than a judge?
    approachable — Executed-replay counterfactuals are implementable with public benchmarks and open models
    from Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
  25. How does the measurability of causal contribution (fraction of decision points with policy-supported counterfactuals) scale with model size, family, and sampling temperature?
    not approachable — Sweeping across frontier-scale policies needs compute the profile lacks, though small-model slices are feasible
    from Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
  26. When credit-rule comparisons are matched on effective sample size and optimizer steps, does any credit rule yield genuine training gains over the untrained policy?
    approachable — Fine-tuning small open models on ALFWorld-scale tasks is within reach of modest compute
    from Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
  27. Does the observed coupling between implicit credit signals and policy fluency produce systematic biases when many agents are trained on each other's judgements at scale?
    approachable — Testable with a self-hosted simulation of iterated judge-and-train loops using small models
    from Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
  28. Does the finding that external distillation adds genuinely new problem solutions while self-training does not hold across model families and scales, or is it specific to an 8B model with rank-32 LoRA?
    approachable — LoRA self-training on open small/mid-size checkpoints plus public benchmarks is feasible on modest GPU budgets
    from Phantom Gains: Auditing Self-Improvement Against a Measured Null
  29. How many baseline replicates are actually required for a measured-null transition audit to be reliable, and can a cheaper replicate-allocation design achieve the same false-discovery control?
    approachable — can be studied by resampling repeated evaluation runs of one open model, no new large training needed
    from Phantom Gains: Auditing Self-Improvement Against a Measured Null
  30. How much of the spurious per-problem capability change attributed to inference batching persists across serving stacks, batch sizes and decoding settings, and can it be eliminated by deterministic serving configurations?
    approachable — needs only public inference frameworks and repeated decodes on public benchmarks
    from Phantom Gains: Auditing Self-Improvement Against a Measured Null
  31. Is the observation that self-training corrupts previously solved problems above the measured noise floor stable over more rounds of self-training, and does it compound or saturate?
    approachable — additional LoRA rounds on an open 8B model plus the paper's exact-test procedure are within a single-researcher compute budget
    from Phantom Gains: Auditing Self-Improvement Against a Measured Null
  32. Do transition-level measurement artifacts of the kind identified here also inflate reported gains in multi-agent or agent-population self-improvement loops, where per-episode outcomes are differenced across interacting agents?
    approachable — can be tested in a self-written multi-agent simulation with frozen control arms
    from Phantom Gains: Auditing Self-Improvement Against a Measured Null
  33. Does the null-calibrated auditing protocol change the conclusions of already-published self-improvement claims when applied retrospectively to their released artifacts?
    not approachable — most published self-improvement studies do not release the baseline replicates or checkpoints required to reconstruct their nulls
    from Phantom Gains: Auditing Self-Improvement Against a Measured Null
  34. Does a skill library shared across many agents produce behavioural monoculture or correlated failures, and how does that scale with the number of agents drawing on the same induced skills?
    approachable — Can be built as a multi-agent simulation with a shared memory store using public LLM APIs
    from Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
  35. Does a pre-execution skill utility score (combining specificity and abstractness) still predict success when skills are exchanged between heterogeneous agents rather than reused by the same agent?
    approachable — Reimplementable scoring on public benchmark task descriptions with modest API budget
    from Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
  36. What mechanisms or filters should govern which induced skills are admitted to a shared agent memory, given that some retrieved skills degrade performance below a no-memory baseline?
    approachable — Testable by writing an admission-policy layer over an open-source agent benchmark
    from Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
  37. Do the findings that subtask-level and text-format skills transfer better hold across model families, scales, and task domains beyond those tested?
    not approachable — Broad model-family and scale sweeps require compute and engineering beyond a solo few-week effort
    from Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
  38. Beyond a single mid-run surge of safety-critical tasks, which classes of non-stationarity (drifting arrival rates, server failures, adversarial load patterns) open enough headroom for an LLM control plane to beat a static deadline-aware heuristic?
    approachable — released code and seeded instances allow new load-generation regimes in a self-written simulation
    from When Do LLM Agents Help? Deadline-Aware Mixed-Criticality Task Scheduling at the Autonomous-Vehicle Edge
  39. How does the benefit of an LLM control plane over heuristic scheduling scale with the number of edge servers, offloading agents, and concurrent task streams?
    approachable — scaling sweeps are simulation-only, with modest LLM API cost
    from When Do LLM Agents Help? Deadline-Aware Mixed-Criticality Task Scheduling at the Autonomous-Vehicle Edge
  40. Does the LLM control plane's advantage survive comparison with learned adaptive policies (e.g. RL or contextual-bandit variants richer than the tested bandit) under the same non-stationary loads?
    approachable — training small RL/bandit controllers in the released simulator is within stated skills
    from When Do LLM Agents Help? Deadline-Aware Mixed-Criticality Task Scheduling at the Autonomous-Vehicle Edge
  41. Do multiple independently-run LLM control planes bidding in the same contract-net auction produce emergent failure modes such as herding on the same server or implicit collusion against best-effort traffic?
    approachable — multi-agent extension of the public auction simulator is self-implementable
    from When Do LLM Agents Help? Deadline-Aware Mixed-Criticality Task Scheduling at the Autonomous-Vehicle Edge
  42. Are the control-plane latency and monetary cost of LLM orchestration low enough for real deployed vehicular edge systems, as opposed to simulated instances?
    not approachable — requires access to a deployed MEC/vehicle testbed and real traffic traces
    from When Do LLM Agents Help? Deadline-Aware Mixed-Criticality Task Scheduling at the Autonomous-Vehicle Edge
  43. Do the reported gains transfer to real-world autonomous-vehicle offloading traces rather than synthetic topologies and instances?
    not approachable — needs proprietary vehicle/edge workload telemetry
    from When Do LLM Agents Help? Deadline-Aware Mixed-Criticality Task Scheduling at the Autonomous-Vehicle Edge
  44. How do reward-optimised sparse communication topologies scale as the number of agents grows from a handful to hundreds or thousands — does the token saving hold, and does accuracy degrade at scale?
    approachable — Can be tested with a self-written multi-agent harness and public LLM APIs, though API cost limits the largest scales
    from Reward-Guided Autoregressive Graph Generation for Efficient Multi-Agent Communication Topology Design
  45. Do topologies learned with a compactness reward generalise to task distributions unseen during reward-model training, or do they overfit to the benchmark suite?
    approachable — Requires only re-running the open pipeline on additional public benchmarks
    from Reward-Guided Autoregressive Graph Generation for Efficient Multi-Agent Communication Topology Design
  46. Does rewarding sparsity make multi-agent systems more fragile to a single faulty, adversarial, or prompt-injected agent, since fewer redundant communication paths exist?
    approachable — Simulatable by injecting faulty agents into a self-implemented topology harness
    from Reward-Guided Autoregressive Graph Generation for Efficient Multi-Agent Communication Topology Design
  47. What structural signatures (degree distribution, centralisation, information bottlenecks) do reward-guided generators converge to, and does the resulting concentration of information flow through hub agents create population-level failure modes?
    approachable — Network analysis of generated topology logs is within stated network-data skills
    from Reward-Guided Autoregressive Graph Generation for Efficient Multi-Agent Communication Topology Design
  48. Can the reward model's trade-off between task correctness and structural compactness be tuned as a steering knob at deployment time rather than fixed during fine-tuning?
    approachable — Needs only small-scale fine-tuning and reward reweighting, no frontier compute
    from Reward-Guided Autoregressive Graph Generation for Efficient Multi-Agent Communication Topology Design
  49. How large is the policy-misalignment penalty in practice when a finite-memory classical simulator stands in for a long-memory environment — i.e. what is the measured regret of a policy trained in the approximate model versus the true process, as a function of memory size?
    approachable — Can be measured by implementing the stochastic processes and tabular RL agents in a self-written simulation
    from An Irreducible Quantum Advantage in Aligning World Models with Reality
  50. Do learned sequence-model world models (e.g. RNN/transformer or LLM-driven simulators) reproduce the predicted failure signatures — collapse of action distinguishability and persistent expected-reward error — on processes constructed to be classically irreducible?
    approachable — Small-scale training/evaluation on synthetic processes fits public compute and standard ML skills
    from An Irreducible Quantum Advantage in Aligning World Models with Reality
  51. Does the irreducible classical-modelling gap persist, or compound, when many interacting agents are trained inside the same imperfect world model, e.g. producing correlated policy errors or herding across the agent population?
    approachable — Testable by extending the synthetic environment to a multi-agent ABM the researcher can write
    from An Irreducible Quantum Advantage in Aligning World Models with Reality
  52. Can the exact quantum world model be realised on available quantum hardware, and does its alignment advantage survive realistic noise and decoherence?
    not approachable — Requires quantum hardware access and quantum-information expertise the profile does not claim
    from An Irreducible Quantum Advantage in Aligning World Models with Reality
  53. Is there a general characterisation of which real-world environments (as opposed to hand-constructed processes) admit no finite classical world model preserving optimal policies?
    not approachable — Requires new proofs in computational mechanics/quantum information rather than empirical work
    from An Irreducible Quantum Advantage in Aligning World Models with Reality

Part 2 — papers (10)

Pandora's AI Model Routing Box: Efficient Allocation with Costly Value Estimation
Adam Fisch, Shubhendu Trivedi, Fantine Huot, William W. Cohen, Michael Kaisers, Mirella Lapata, Kate Larson, Jacob Eisenstein
2608.20316 · similarity 0.918 to Habermolt: Delegating Deliberation to AI Representatives · significance 4/5 · novelty 4/5
Casts model routing with costly value estimation as a Pandora's Box problem and studies both a centralized router and a decentralized bidding market of specialists.
  • When autonomous specialists each decide whether to invest in self-assessment before bidding for a task, under what conditions does value-of-information reasoning shift surplus from the mechanism to strategic bidders rather than improving allocative efficiency? (approachable: Can be studied in a self-written auction simulation with synthetic Gaussian signals)
  • Do decentralized bidding markets with costly self-assessment remain incentive-compatible and stable when many specialists adopt the same value-of-information policy, or does correlated bidding produce herding and price instability? (approachable: Population-level agent-based simulation of the bidding mechanism is writable in weeks)
  • How do routing policies based on a Gaussian signal model degrade when specialist value distributions are heavy-tailed, correlated across specialists, or nonstationary over time? (approachable: Requires only simulation plus public multi-LLM benchmark scores)
  • Does repeated routing among a fixed pool of specialists cause monoculture, where a few models capture most queries and the diversity benefit of heterogeneous systems erodes? (approachable: Measurable in a longitudinal simulation over public benchmark specialists)
  • Can strategic specialists learn to misreport self-assessments over repeated interactions with a router, and what audit or pricing rules detect such misreporting from allocation logs alone? (approachable: Learning agents against a router can be implemented with open models and small compute)
  • How do these routing and bidding policies perform in a live deployment with real user traffic, latency constraints, and evolving specialist inventories? (not approachable: Needs production serving infrastructure and proprietary traffic data)
What You Can't See Is What You Learn: Restricted Evidence Visibility Favors Compositional Generalization in Shared-Genome Language-Model Societies
Narcis Marincat
2608.20054 · similarity 0.917 to Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web · significance 4/5 · novelty 4/5
Trains four-cell societies of language-model agents sharing one adapter and shows that restricting each cell's evidence visibility increases the chance of a compositionally generalizing communication interface.
  • Does restricting evidence visibility among communicating LLM modules still favor generalizing, reusable interfaces as the number of agents grows well beyond four cells, and how does the effect scale with society size and relay topology? (approachable: Small frozen-LM plus LoRA societies can be re-implemented and scaled modestly on public models with modest compute)
  • Do the value-indexed, transplantable communication packets that emerge under restricted visibility survive in non-fixed, learned or dynamic communication topologies rather than a fixed relay? (approachable: Requires only modifying the relay/attention mask in a self-written training setup)
  • Why did all trained societies fail ordinary-language preservation, and can training protocols be found that retain general language ability while acquiring a compositional relay interface? (not approachable: Diagnosing and repairing degradation of general language ability likely needs larger-scale training and evaluation infrastructure)
  • Can the intervention battery used here (same-value packet transplants, destructive ablations, counterfactual packets) be developed into a general observability method for auditing whether inter-agent messages in larger multi-agent systems carry reusable, semantically indexed content? (approachable: Method transfer and evaluation on open multi-agent frameworks needs only public models and simulation code)
  • Would the restricted-visibility advantage replicate on tasks other than sealed natural-language function composition, and does it hold above the preregistered accuracy floor with different base models? (approachable: New task suites and open base models are publicly available; compute needs are small with frozen LM plus adapter)
Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
Chenchen Lin, Wenhao Yuan, Xuehe Wang, Edith Cheuk Han Ngai
2608.19701 · similarity 0.915 to Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web · significance 4/5 · novelty 4/5
Identifies correlated provenance among memories written by different agents as a source of false majorities and proposes a framework estimating effective independent evidence before arbitration.
  • How does memory correlation bias scale as the number of agents sharing a memory store grows — does the false-majority effect worsen superlinearly with population size and shared upstream sources? (approachable: Can be studied with a self-written multi-agent memory simulation over synthetic provenance graphs)
  • Can memory correlation bias, and the effective number of independent evidence sources, be measured from interaction/provenance logs alone as a monitoring signal for a deployed multi-agent system? (approachable: Requires only logs from a locally run agent system plus network/statistical analysis)
  • Does correlation-aware arbitration reduce population-level pathologies such as herding, information cascades and belief monoculture, beyond improving per-query benchmark accuracy? (approachable: Testable in an agent-based simulation with shared memory, no proprietary data needed)
  • How robust is provenance-based correlation estimation to adversarial agents that forge or launder provenance metadata to manufacture apparent independence? (approachable: Adversarial agents can be scripted in a simulated memory-sharing environment)
  • What is the retrieval-cost versus arbitration-reliability trade-off of active evidence recovery when applied across thousands of agents and long time horizons? (not approachable: Long-horizon large-population LLM agent runs need substantial inference compute budget)
Distilling Aggregate Mobility Statistics into a Language Model Policy for Post-Event Crowd Simulation
Tatsuya Amano, Hirozumi Yamaguchi
2608.19778 · similarity 0.912 to AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society · significance 4/5 · novelty 4/5
Fine-tunes a language-model pedestrian agent policy so that simulated destination composition matches aggregate mobile-network origin-destination flows, using iterative proportional fitting and resampled training data.
  • Does distilling aggregate destination composition into an LLM agent policy generalise beyond stadium egress after sporting events, to other event types, cities, or transport modes? (approachable: public OD/mobility datasets and open LLM fine-tuning at small scale suffice for a replication study)
  • How much individual-level behavioural realism is recoverable from aggregate counts alone, and what identifiability limits govern which behaviour rules are distinguishable given only zone counts and OD flows? (approachable: can be studied by generating synthetic ground-truth trajectories in a self-written simulator and testing recovery)
  • Are there correction schemes better than iterative proportional fitting plus resampled fine-tuning for counteracting the dominant-class inflation introduced by fine-tuning on aggregate targets? (approachable: small LoRA fine-tuning experiments on open models are within reach of a single researcher)
  • Does matching aggregate destination shares also improve downstream simulation outcomes such as congestion, crowd density peaks, or evacuation times, rather than only the fitted statistic? (approachable: requires only a pedestrian simulator the researcher can write and public event data)
  • How does the calibrated crowd policy behave when many such agents interact and adapt to congestion, i.e. do aggregate-fitted policies remain valid under endogenous crowd feedback? (approachable: multi-agent simulation loop is implementable locally)

Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
Haiyue Zhang
2608.19760 · similarity 0.912 to LLM economicus? Mapping the Behavioral Biases of LLMs via Utility Theory · significance 4/5 · novelty 4/5
Audits step-level credit signals for LLM agents against counterfactual replay ground truth and finds none identifies causally pivotal steps better than chance.
  • Do step-level credit signals (LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, policy confidence) fail to track causal contribution in multi-agent or multi-turn interactive environments as they do in a single-agent tool environment? (approachable: Can be run with open-weight agents in a public multi-agent simulation the researcher writes)
  • Can a credit-assignment signal be constructed that beats chance at identifying causally pivotal decision points, e.g. by using cheap partial replay rather than a judge? (approachable: Executed-replay counterfactuals are implementable with public benchmarks and open models)
  • How does the measurability of causal contribution (fraction of decision points with policy-supported counterfactuals) scale with model size, family, and sampling temperature? (not approachable: Sweeping across frontier-scale policies needs compute the profile lacks, though small-model slices are feasible)
  • When credit-rule comparisons are matched on effective sample size and optimizer steps, does any credit rule yield genuine training gains over the untrained policy? (approachable: Fine-tuning small open models on ALFWorld-scale tasks is within reach of modest compute)

Phantom Gains: Auditing Self-Improvement Against a Measured Null
Cheng Xu, Nan Yan, Liming Chen, M-Tahar Kechadi
2608.20290 · similarity 0.919 to Retrieval Collapses When AI Pollutes the Web · significance 3/5 · novelty 4/5
Audits per-problem gain/loss statistics used to claim LLM self-improvement against measured null baselines and shows seven measurement artifacts that invert reported findings.
  • Does the finding that external distillation adds genuinely new problem solutions while self-training does not hold across model families and scales, or is it specific to an 8B model with rank-32 LoRA? (approachable: LoRA self-training on open small/mid-size checkpoints plus public benchmarks is feasible on modest GPU budgets)
  • How many baseline replicates are actually required for a measured-null transition audit to be reliable, and can a cheaper replicate-allocation design achieve the same false-discovery control? (approachable: can be studied by resampling repeated evaluation runs of one open model, no new large training needed)
  • How much of the spurious per-problem capability change attributed to inference batching persists across serving stacks, batch sizes and decoding settings, and can it be eliminated by deterministic serving configurations? (approachable: needs only public inference frameworks and repeated decodes on public benchmarks)
  • Is the observation that self-training corrupts previously solved problems above the measured noise floor stable over more rounds of self-training, and does it compound or saturate? (approachable: additional LoRA rounds on an open 8B model plus the paper's exact-test procedure are within a single-researcher compute budget)
  • Do transition-level measurement artifacts of the kind identified here also inflate reported gains in multi-agent or agent-population self-improvement loops, where per-episode outcomes are differenced across interacting agents? (approachable: can be tested in a self-written multi-agent simulation with frozen control arms)
  • Does the null-calibrated auditing protocol change the conclusions of already-published self-improvement claims when applied retrospectively to their released artifacts? (not approachable: most published self-improvement studies do not release the baseline replicates or checkpoints required to reconstruct their nulls)
Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
Yiyang Feng, Biddut Sarker Bijoy, Niranjan Balasubramanian, Jiawei Zhou
2608.20274 · similarity 0.918 to AgentScope 1.0: A Developer-Centric Framework for Building Agentic Applications · significance 3/5 · novelty 3/5
Compares task-level versus subtask-level and text versus code skill induction for cross-task transfer among LLM agents and proposes a skill utility score predicting transfer success.
  • Does a skill library shared across many agents produce behavioural monoculture or correlated failures, and how does that scale with the number of agents drawing on the same induced skills? (approachable: Can be built as a multi-agent simulation with a shared memory store using public LLM APIs)
  • Does a pre-execution skill utility score (combining specificity and abstractness) still predict success when skills are exchanged between heterogeneous agents rather than reused by the same agent? (approachable: Reimplementable scoring on public benchmark task descriptions with modest API budget)
  • What mechanisms or filters should govern which induced skills are admitted to a shared agent memory, given that some retrieved skills degrade performance below a no-memory baseline? (approachable: Testable by writing an admission-policy layer over an open-source agent benchmark)
  • Do the findings that subtask-level and text-format skills transfer better hold across model families, scales, and task domains beyond those tested? (not approachable: Broad model-family and scale sweeps require compute and engineering beyond a solo few-week effort)
When Do LLM Agents Help? Deadline-Aware Mixed-Criticality Task Scheduling at the Autonomous-Vehicle Edge
Reza Zakerian
2608.19557 · similarity 0.914 to Prompt Infection: LLM-to-LLM Prompt Injection within Multi-Agent Systems · significance 3/5 · novelty 3/5
Compares a contract-net auction heuristic and a multi-agent LLM control plane for deadline-aware mixed-criticality task scheduling at the vehicular edge, finding LLM benefit only under non-stationary load.
